item.title: Commentary: Mayor McDonald Looks Beyond City Hall's Turmoil Toward a Bigger Vision for Alamogordo
item.description:
Last weekend, the world came to southern New Mexico. For four days in October, the 30th XTERRA World Championship filled Ruidoso with elite athletes, young racers and their families from across the globe. They swam in Grindstone Lake, raced over mountain trails beneath Sierra Blanca, and crowned world champions in a village of about 7,000 people that has spent recent years recovering from wildfire and flooding.

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald was there. She didn't go to race or make speeches. She went to observe and to learn. She met athletes from around the world, talked with families and organizers, and paid close attention to what it takes for a small mountain community to host an international event.

It was a telling choice of where to spend her time.

Above the noise

Anyone following Alamogordo city government knows it has been a difficult stretch. City hall has moved from one controversy to the next, bogged down by personnel disputes and the threat of lawsuits, millions in payouts with more eminent. A recent employee firing resulting in yet another potential FMLA violation and a new EEOC investigation. Those issues are real, a direct reflection of the city managers office and must be resolved.

But a city cannot be defined by its internal disputes, and its political leaders cannot spend all their energy on them.

Mayor McDonald has chosen to step above that day-to-day dysfunction and focus on something bigger: a vision for what Alamogordo could become.

That distinction matters, because local government has two jobs that are often confused. Roads, water lines and infrastructure are essential priorities, and implementing them is the responsibility of the city manager and staff

Elected leaders and more importantly the mayors as outlined in the city charter have a different role: to set direction, learn from others, build relationships and inspire the community about its future. Mayor McDonald is doing exactly that.

The lesson from up the mountain

Ruidoso offers a clear example of what vision can accomplish. A village a fraction of Alamogordo's size convinced a global sports brand to bring its world championship there for three straight years, through 2028. It did so by selling what it already had: landscape, trails, hospitality and a community willing to show up.

It also did not happen overnight. Ruidoso hosted a test event in 2025, proved it could deliver, and earned the world's attention. Opportunities are built step by step, through relationships and a willingness to try.

What Alamogordo already has

Alamogordo does not need to invent an identity. It already has assets many communities would envy.

White Sands National Park sits at our doorstep, one of the most striking landscapes in the country. The Sacramento Mountains and Lincoln National Forest rise just to the east. Within the city, plentiful parks offer space for races, festivals and family gatherings. A downtown business corridor in the middle of revitalization gives visitors somewhere to eat, shop and linger.

Put together, those assets describe a destination: desert and mountains, national park and small-town main street, all within a short drive.

Building relationships across the region

Ruidoso was only one stop. Mayor McDonald plans to attend the state's outdoor recreation conference to continue learning. She is also meeting with state legislators, legislative candidates, mayors of neighboring cities and state leaders, making the case that Alamogordo is eager to host events and grow tourism.

Closer to home, she works closely with the leadership of the Sacramento Mountain Foundation and the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce, connecting city hall with the people who know our mountains, our businesses and our visitors best.

That regional approach may be the most important lesson of all. Ruidoso did not land a world championship alone. Alamogordo and its neighbors in the Tularosa Basin and Sacramento Mountains are not competitors for a single prize. Each strengthens the case for the others, and a visitor drawn to one is likely to discover the rest. Collaboration breeds ideas, and ideas breed success.

A vision for tourism and small business

The goal is to have event organizers, travelers and entrepreneurs see Alamogordo not as a place to pass through, but as a place to come to. Trail runs on the edge of the dunes, cycling events climbing into the mountains, and festivals in our parks and downtown are all within reach if we pursue them deliberately.

Tourism and events bring more than weekend crowds. They fill restaurants and hotels, support the small businesses that make up our downtown, create jobs and give residents reasons to take pride in where they live. They also draw the attention that leads to broader economic development.

Time to step into the spotlight

City hall's disputes will eventually be settled, and the roads will be repaired. But a city also needs someone looking past the next agenda item to ask what it could become.

Mayor McDonald is asking that question. She is seeking ideas, meeting with leaders across the region and the state, and building a vision of Alamogordo as more than it is today: a destination worthy of visitors, tourism and investment. That vision deserves the community's attention, and its support. That is leadership above the fold and that is exactly what Alamogordo needs now to grow and thrive. Stay tuned as a visionary leader establishes goals and objectives for the region.

item.title: Tonight's LEDA Vote: Leadership or Politics?
item.description:
Tonight at 6:30, City Manager Robert Stockwell faces his first real test, and so does the four-member commission majority that hired him.

Alamogordo has watched this before. Three city managers in a row brought professional recommendations to this commission. Three times, the majority decided insider politics mattered more. Tonight's LEDA vote will show whether this commission lets its new manager manage, or whether it overrides him the way it overrode the last three.

The commission will decide what to do with roughly $1 million in LEDA money. It is the last the city expects to see, because the gross receipts tax that funded the program has been rededicated.

Stockwell's recommendation is clear. Pass over all five business applications and put the money into cleaning up and demolishing dilapidated buildings. White Sands Boulevard comes first, then East Tenth Street, East First Street and residential properties next to commercial zones.

He would do it with the Chamber of Commerce and the Sacramento Mountains Foundation, which has committed its own money to the effort. His fallback option is to award the full balance to one applicant: Pymo Bistro & Hotel, downtown in the historic Avis Building.

Fix the front door. Anyone who drives into town on White Sands Boulevard knows what investors see. Stockwell's report says every conversation about Alamogordo's economic future comes back to its image. One-time money should fix a problem that is holding back every future deal, not prop up one business.

Stretch every dollar. Pairing city money with foundation money means more buildings cleaned up and torn down than public money could manage alone. Foundation dollars also carry fewer restrictions on private property, which frees city funds for code enforcement. Stockwell's report states the use is allowed under LEDA.

Look at the track record. Stockwell concluded that LEDA projects here have produced little sustained job creation or revenue growth. That is the same standard Dr. Stephanie Hernandez applied as acting city manager: LEDA is about jobs and return, not favors. Last year staff recommended about $475,000 for a local gym. Commissioners pushed for far more, the fight turned ugly, and the applicant withdrew. That same gym is back this year asking for $1 million.

If it must be a business, it should be Pymo. Of the five applicants, Stockwell found only Pymo would meaningfully move gross receipts tax revenue. We agree wholeheartedly. Its owner has already invested heavily in restoring a historic downtown building. But the commission should demand complete financials first: Pymo's packet says those will be "provided in person," and its $1.3 million request is larger than the money available. Do it right, or don't do it.

LEDA is $1 million. The real money is $160 million. In 2024 the city approved water and sewer rate increases that climb every year through 2032 to pay for $160.4 million in critical repairs. Residents are paying that bill right now, every month.

Stockwell did not inherit an empty pipeline. When Dr. Hernandez left, she said several projects were ready to go with funding already identified, and simply needed to be put out. The city had about $28 million in approved water and sewer funding and roughly $12 million in financing for the aquatic center.

Area contractors were told bidding would pick up once the new city manager arrived. He started July 1. Three and a half months later, the one major new bid on the street is the aquatic center, posted September 25 and closing December 15. Meanwhile roads and water lines keep crumbling, and water bills keep rising.

Stockwell was hired on the strength of decades of experience, at a $180,000 base salary. He was not presented as someone who needed months to learn Alamogordo. The public, the ratepayers and the contractors waiting to bid are owed a schedule.

Tonight tests the commission. Will the four-member majority back the professional recommendation of the manager it hired 5-2, or override him for insiders again?

Tonight also tests Stockwell. Will he stand behind his own recommendation if the majority pushes back? And will he give residents a public bid calendar for the funded water, sewer and road projects, with dates, within 30 days?

Politics or leadership. We'll be watching. Join us at the 6:30 p.m. meeting in the Commission Chambers at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St. Sign up with the City Clerk before the meeting to speak; you'll get about three minutes.

item.title: Jury Finds Alamogordo Man Guilty in 2023 Kidnapping of Former Friend
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Ernesto Robles faces up to 27 years in prison after an Otero County jury found him guilty of first-degree kidnapping and conspiracy to commit first-degree kidnapping, according to the Twelfth Judicial District Attorney's Office, which announced the verdict Tuesday. He is scheduled to be sentenced Nov. 13.

Prosecutors say Robles was one of four people who took a woman from her Alamogordo home on June 10, 2023. The victim had once been friends with the group, according to the district attorney's office. The other three were identified as Vanessa Renteria, Samantha Martinez and Luis Balderas.

According to prosecutors, the woman was beaten while being driven to Robles' residence and was threatened with a gun. Once there, she was bound and gagged in a wheelchair, beaten further, and had part of her head shaved.

The district attorney's office said threats made against the woman and her relatives kept her from going to authorities right away.

Two co-defendants have already been sentenced after pleading guilty. Renteria admitted to second-degree kidnapping and bribery of a witness and was sentenced July 14 to 21 years in prison. Martinez pleaded guilty to second-degree kidnapping and received 18 years on July 29.

item.title: City Manager Stockwell blames past design for project delays, but the same engineering firms are still on the job
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — City Manager Robert Stockwell told the City Commission this week that the city's recent infrastructure projects ran over schedule and piled up change orders because they were "insufficiently designed" and "rushed to bid." He said he has directed staff to hold new projects until they are "really ready to go."

The projects he singled out were designed by contracted, on-call engineering firms, not city staff. Those firms are still working for the city. One such firm just launched design work on the city's new aquatic center and is attached to several other projects now waiting on Stockwell's review.

This raises a question his explanation did not answer. If the old designs were the problem, what has changed now that the same firms are doing the new work?

Stockwell spoke near the end of the meeting. He said he was responding to social media criticism that the city has been slow to bid capital projects since he arrived about 90 days ago. He said he does not read those posts himself.

"I think it needs to be reminded when we look at the recent experience that the city has had, like on the reconstruction of Oregon Avenue, a project that should have been completed in months took over a year, had multiple change orders because the project was improperly designed, well, insufficiently designed, bid out, and then multiple change orders over the months," Stockwell said.

He went on to criticize three more projects:

"What I have directed staff to do, and why you are not seeing projects coming forward right now, is … take a very close look at all of the projects that are already in the design and preparing to go to bid, so that we don't make those same kind of mistakes again," he said.

He also said contractors who expect to profit from change orders are "the kind of contractors we don't want." He closed with: "If that means I'm not very good at my job, then I'll take that."

Stockwell did not name any engineering firm or say what specific design flaws he had found. He also gave no dates for when the projects under review would go to bid.

According to people familiar with the city's capital program, the only recent project designed in-house by city staff was White Sands Boulevard to 1st Street. Oregon Avenue Phase 1, the 10th Street culvert, Great Blocks and Fire Station 2 were all designed through the city's on-call engineering contracts.

Those contracts are still in place. The same contracted firms also designed projects that are now on hold, including Granada Hills, the well transmission line and Oregon Avenue Phase 2. Oregon Phase 2 has already had four design walkthroughs.

Stockwell has also presented contracted project management as an improvement. However, the city already paid for professional construction-management services on earlier projects, including Oregon Phase 1.

Commission records show that much of the extra work Stockwell described as design failure was scope the city added during construction.

In several cases the commission approved those additions unanimously.

Oregon Avenue Phase 1. The street was designed before voters approved the pool. Once the natatorium went ahead, the city chose to add water and sewer service for it during construction instead of cutting into a brand-new street later with approval by the very commissioners now questioning the decisions that they encouraged.

The two change orders were:

They added 60 and 149 days. The second order cited weather, unmarked utilities and the need to keep a traffic corridor open. It passed unanimously by this very set of  commissioners via multiple votes and approvals. 

10th Street culvert. The city knew the structure had problems. A crack under the bridge had gone unaddressed for about a decade and was an emergency due to failure to properly inspect bridges and a failure of the commission for over a decade in oversight. Staff were facing a grant deadline, and commissioners were pressing to reopen the road. The project's one change order was $43,850 to relocate a 10-inch reclaimed-water line that was not where the plans showed it. It was approved 6–0. The work was funded as a repair. Full replacement of the bridge was never in the budget.

Great Blocks. The project began several city managers ago with state MainStreet money that had a deadline. Staff publicly acknowledged at the time that the inherited design was weak. Its largest change order was $605,627.55 for a pedestrian hybrid beacon, one-way signage, striping, sidewalks and alley work. That work was added after public pressure over the traffic changes; it was not in the original design. Flooding concerns were raised during construction, not recently. Staff met with the engineer, the contractor and affected businesses. The city refused to consider correcting the issue. Requests for further fixes were limited by the finance department. The city project manager at the time had no authority to make the suggested fixes. The city is now facing possible litigation in the termination of that project manager under questionable circumstances and a potential claim by the business owners for damages to their building and merchandise due to flooding as a result of the city failing to act preemptively even after being notified. The responsibility of the flooding clearly was recognized and the finance department and the commission ignored the issue. 

Fire Station 2. The city moved funding for this project from an Indian Wells-area station to a fire administration building and finally to Fire Station 2, with a state deadline approaching. The design went through departmental and state review. The $83,068.08 change order for apparatus-bay doors drew the most criticism. City staff had planned to buy the doors through an existing purchasing agreement. Finance instead required them to go through the construction contract. A third change order of $143,368.79 was tabled Sept. 8.

Several commissioners praised Stockwell's remarks and failed to accept responsibility for their votes and their role in the change orders. Those very commissioners also approved the change orders and extensions now being cited as evidence of poor planning. Some of them pushed staff to finish faster and reopen streets sooner. In the case of 10th Street, that included visiting the site.

Under the most recent city manager Dr Hernandez, the city completed 22 capital projects. Stockwell's remarks did not mention them and paints a view that is not supported by the record of projects completed or public funds expended. 

Local contractors have told this outlet they are frustrated by the pause and the Stockwell narrative is not reality and not what Commissioners Rardin, Burnett and Patillo promised them. They say several projects that appear ready to bid have no schedule and the explanations on delays are not truthful. 

Citizens are getting more and more upset as the increased expenses of water and sanitation collections pile into the city coffers and roads and infrastructure continue to deteriorate with false narratives and false promises by an embattled city manager that was supposed to move projects forward quickly. 

Stockwell says the pause will prevent repeat mistakes. He has not said what deficiencies the review has found in the current designs, what is being corrected, or when any of the held projects will go out to bid.

The International City/County Management Association's code of ethics calls on members to show professional respect for colleagues, including predecessors, Stockwell’s MO appears to be to blame predecessors versus owning the issues at hand. Meanwhile citizens are frustrated, water bills increase and roads continue to deteriorate all the while the city faces even more employee turmoil and potential litigation.

Stay turned for a litigation update in the upcoming weeks and it’s expected cost to taxpayers as a result of this administration’s actions.

item.title: Block told voters his lawsuit was “resolved.” A judge set it for trial. Now a PAC tied to his news site is mailing his opponent’s 2008 record
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — On April 2, Rep. John Block told his constituents the lawsuit filed against him by his former domestic partner “has since been resolved amicably between the parties, and any claims otherwise are false.”

On July 13, District Judge Lori L. Gibson Willard denied Block’s two motions to throw the case out and set it for a four-day trial beginning March 30, 2027.

This week, with that trial on the calendar, a political action committee that shares an address with Block’s Piñon Post — and that writes checks to it — mailed District 51 voters a flyer about his opponent’s criminal record. It ends in 2008.

The mailer, paid for by Piñon PAC, lists Independent candidate Grace Nagamine’s convictions and no-contest pleas from 2005 to 2008 and calls her “too dangerous to be state representative.” A review of New Mexico court records shows no criminal case against Nagamine in the 18 years since. 

Nagamine, 

Nagamine , a mother of seven and founder of the Alamogordo nonprofit Royal Angels, has never disputed the record. She published it herself. Her memoir, The Grace Nagamine Story, released in August, describes those years — domestic abuse, addiction, homelessness, and a short jail term — in her own words. The campaign says it has handed out several hundred copies across Otero County, and the book was in circulation two months before the mailer was.

“I’ve never hidden my past, including the charges from my past, and I never will,” Nagamine said in a video released Tuesday. “I wrote an entire book about my life, including the mistakes I’ve made, the charges I’ve faced, and the struggles I’ve overcome. I’ve given away hundreds of copies throughout my campaign because I have nothing to hide.”

“If my opponent believes that bringing up my past, including my past charges, will somehow silence me, embarrass me or discourage me, he is mistaken.”

A link to her video can be found at https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1R5c4wrcao/?mibextid=wwXIfr

Eighteen years

The hit piece mailer’s framing — a two-decade-old record presented as current danger — drew sharp public reaction within hours of the video’s release, much of it from people who said they had read the book.

“All of this is clearly explained in her book,” wrote Stephanie Pacheco Hernandez in a public comment on social media. “While John may think he is attacking Grace, he is really attacking every person who is trying to rebuild their life after hardship. He is sending the message that no matter how much work you do, no matter how much you grow, you should forever be judged by your worst moments.”

“I met Grace and got a copy of her book. She’s quite open about her life,” wrote a response. “John Block could take a lesson about honesty from her.”

One District 51 voter texted the campaign after receiving the mailer: “After that super crappy ad that I got today in the mail that was not kind to you, I suggest you come put 10 signs in my yard, or maybe 20.”

Nagamine’s campaign said the mailer is designed to change the subject. “Rep. Block has had four years in Santa Fe,” the campaign said in a statement. “If he had a record he was proud of, he’d be mailing voters that.”

“Resolved amicably”

The record Block is not mailing includes his own case presently active in the courts. 

In Melton v. Block, No. D-1215-CV-2025-00757, 12th Judicial District Court, Otero County Treasurer Karl P. Melton alleges Block breached a written agreement, signed Nov. 7, 2024, governing shared property after the end of their gay four-year domestic partnership. Block has counterclaimed that the property — including family heirlooms — is his.

The timeline, from the docket:

— Dec. 19, 2025 — Block moves for summary judgment on a loan claim.

— April 2, 2026 — Block posts on his official Facebook page that the suit was “a private property dispute that has since been resolved amicably between the parties, and any claims otherwise are false.” The same day, his attorney sends this newspaper a cease-and-desist letter demanding retraction of its reporting on the case and the identity of its confidential sources. The story remains. 

— May 28, 2026 — Block files an emergency motion asking the court to strike a Melton filing, impose up to $5,000 in sanctions, seal the filing and its exhibits, and enter a protective order barring Melton “or anyone acting in concert with him” from disseminating its contents. The motion names this newspaper and the Eddy and Lea County Exposed newsletter.

— July 13, 2026 — Judge Gibson Willard denies both summary-judgment motions, strikes and seals the single Melton filing because of attached text messages, declines to seal the case — “Not sealing entire case, not sealing future motions; just saying be careful what you attach” — defers sanctions to trial, and sets trial for March 30–April 2, 2027.

Block has not publicly corrected his April 2 false statement.

Block’s filings describe Melton’s motion as “scandalous and impertinent” and categorically deny an affair alleged in it. His attorney, Michael J. Seibel, argued the material was irrelevant to a dispute over household goods and was filed to embarrass his client.

The cease-and-desist letter to this newspaper is now part of the record in a State Ethics Commission complaint against Block, Case No. 2026-016. No lawsuit against the newspaper has been filed. The Eddy and Lea County Exposed newsletter, which has published filings from the case, recently reached a $100,000 settlement in a separate public-records matter and continues to cover Blocks antics. 

The committee behind the mailer

Piñon PAC is not an outside group. Its disclaimer lists 1111 Tenth St. #402, Alamogordo, the same street address used by Pinon Post LLC, the company behind the Piñon Post, which Block founded and edits.

The money runs in a circle. According to Transparency USA’s compilation of New Mexico campaign finance filings, Piñon PAC paid Pinon Post LLC $2,336.90 on April 15, 2026, and another $2,336.90 on June 4 — $4,673.80 in all. Both payments are categorized only as “Other,” with the description “Monetary Itemized: Check.” No purpose is disclosed. Block’s own campaign committee, John for New Mexico, has in turn paid Piñon PAC $2,000 and the PAC has reimbursed Block personally for literature/mailings per Transparency USA. 

Karl Melton — the plaintiff suing Block — served as treasurer of Piñon PAC / John for New Mexico until early 2025, Secretary of State records show.. It reported roughly $31,600 on hand at the end of June.

In other words: Block’s campaign funds the PAC among other donations, the PAC pays Block’s news site and Block himself, and the PAC’s mailer attacks Block’s opponent — with the PAC, not Block, named on the disclaimer. Neither Block, the PAC, nor Pinon Post LLC has issued statements about who directs the committee’s spending or what the payments to Pinon Post LLC were for. An inquiry is being filed with the SOS and IPRA requests. 

The contrast

Nagamine’s legal history is 18 years old, self-published, and closed. Block’s is current, contested, and set for trial five months after Election Day — and he has spent the past six months asking a court to keep parts of it out of public view while telling voters it was over.

Election Day is Nov. 3. Early voting in Otero County began. Civility is what matters in elections, let’s stop the hate and address the issues voters really care about: safe communities, affordability, roads and infrastructure.

item.title: Voting Matters and Why We Need to See the Bigger Picture
item.description:
When we elect officials, whether at the federal, state, or local level, we tend to focus on what they will do within their individual offices. But I think we should also ask another question: How willing are they to work with other government entities for the benefit of the communities they serve?

Our city, county, and schools have very different responsibilities, budgets, and challenges. Each has its own mission. Yet they serve many of the same people. The family experiences the community, even when government operates in separate pieces.

My stance has always been to work together when we can. That requires respecting each entity’s responsibilities while recognizing where cooperation can improve people’s lives.

Where responsibilities overlap

At the employee level, collaboration often happens naturally and with little public attention. A school resource officer may work for a municipal police department or county sheriff’s office while serving on a school campus. Police officers, firefighters, and emergency medical personnel coordinate at incidents because the situation requires it.

Emergency preparedness should be paramount in these relationships. A wildfire, flood, or school emergency can require coordinated transportation, evacuation routes, shelters, communications, and family reunification. We should be planning those responsibilities together before an emergency tests them.

The overlap extends to everyday services. Road repairs affect school access and bus routes. Sidewalks, drainage, and pedestrian crossings affect whether students can get to school safely. Schools and recreation departments can explore shared fields and facilities, with clear agreements about scheduling, costs, and maintenance.

Economic development also connects these institutions.

Opportunities at the Local Level

There are opportunities we can create by being more intentional about these connections. If the city and county are working to attract businesses or improve infrastructure, we should also ask how our schools can help students prepare for the jobs those efforts may generate. Schools can introduce career pathways, while local government departments provide internships, mentorship, and practical experience.

For example, a water-system improvement could become an opportunity to introduce students to engineering, water operations, accounting, or skilled trades. Students interested in public safety could explore those careers through programs such as the Ferguson Academy. County departments could explore similar partnerships based on their workforce needs.

These connections can help students see a future for themselves here. Economic development should include preparing the next generation to participate in, benefit from, and eventually lead the community we are building.

Unfortunately, politics and personalities sometimes get in the way. I have seen situations where the question becomes who gets the credit rather than what is best for the community. If employees can recognize the need to work across organizational boundaries, why shouldn’t we expect the same from elected leadership?

Research helps explain why leadership matters. Ansell and Gash (2008) reviewed 137 cases of collaborative governance and identified factors including leadership, prior conflict or cooperation, and differences in power and resources. Their research concerns broader public and private partnerships, but it offers a useful lesson for local government: cooperation requires attention to relationships and how decisions are made.

Working together still requires accountability. Each entity should understand its responsibilities, what it is contributing, and how the partnership’s results will be evaluated.

Preparing future public servants

When I was city manager, one of my priorities was getting our departments more involved with our schools. I encouraged, and in some instances required, that engagement for two reasons.

First, we faced workforce challenges. I wanted students to understand that local government offers careers ranging from professional positions to skilled trades. There are opportunities in accounting, engineering, technology, public safety, water operations, recreation, and maintenance. Students cannot consider careers they have never been shown.

The Ferguson Academy and our internship programs reflected that thinking. Over two years, approximately 30 students graduated from the Ferguson Academy. The academy connected Alamogordo Public Schools and the city through public safety career exploration. Internships gave students opportunities to experience the work of government and learn from the people providing those services.

I wanted young people to discover their interests and recognize that they could have a future here. We should be asking who will provide our public services tomorrow and what we are doing today to help prepare them.

Second, I wanted young people to understand that government belongs to them, too. I often referred to children as our “silent citizens.” They cannot vote yet, but decisions affecting their lives are often made without input from them. We should never minimize their interests in our planning simply because they cannot vote yet.

Making participation accessible

Kahne and Sporte (2008) help put this concern into context. Their article discusses how economic advantage can translate into a stronger civic voice. Their study also found that family discussions about public issues and civically responsive neighborhoods supported students’ commitment to participation. Young people arrive at school with different opportunities to experience civic life. The researchers also found that civic learning opportunities in school were associated with stronger commitments to civic participation.

For me, the implication is clear: partnering with schools can help reduce barriers tied to wealth and access. Students should have opportunities to participate regardless of their family’s income, connections, or involvement in politics. We can show them that they have a role in shaping government decisions and that the outcomes can belong to them, too.

That was the thinking behind our partnership with APS to let high school students vote on an event designed specifically for them. They had four choices, and their votes determined the outcome: Winter Wonderland at the Zoo, paid for by the city.

It was a simple exercise, but it demonstrated something important: Their voices mattered. They made a choice and could see the result. I wanted them to experience that connection before they were old enough to cast a ballot in a public election.

Those opportunities should not end with a single event. That is one reason I was excited when Mayor McDonald asked me to serve on the Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission. With the students now sworn in, I look forward to mentoring them as they learn more about their community and contribute their perspectives.

I have always had a genuine love and appreciation for education and children. Serving as city manager allowed me to bring that commitment into public service. Our young people are future public servants and voting citizens, and they are members of our community whose voices matter right now.

Collaboration across levels of government

The same thinking extends beyond our city, county, and schools. State and federal officials can help connect local priorities with funding, programs, and technical assistance. Local leaders bring knowledge of community needs and responsibility for carrying projects forward. Their ability to work together can shape the opportunities available to our residents.

Alamogordo has examples of these connections. Through the Community Development Block Grant program, federal funding goes to New Mexico, and the city can apply through the state for eligible infrastructure, housing, and economic-development projects (City of Alamogordo, n.d.). Holloman’s school liaison also connects military families with Alamogordo Public Schools and community resources (Paczkowski, 2024).

The diagram below illustrates where these relationships can create opportunities. It gives us another way to evaluate candidates for state and federal office: Will they understand our local needs and work with community leaders to help address them?

Diagram examples draw on City of Alamogordo (n.d.), New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions (n.d.), New Mexico State University Alamogordo (n.d.), and Paczkowski (2024).

What we should ask of candidates

This brings me back to elections. The people we elect at all levels of government make decisions that affect more than their individual agencies. Their willingness to collaborate can influence emergency preparedness, economic development, workforce opportunities, and the future of our children.

As we head to the polls, we should ask: How do these candidates approach working with other entities? What have they done to support partnerships? Can they put differences aside and work together for the good of the community, even when someone else receives the credit?

An “R” or a “D” does not answer those questions. A candidate’s record, priorities, and willingness to collaborate tell us more.

Our city, county, and schools may have different responsibilities, but our citizens depend on all three. The decisions we make at the ballot box affect the services we receive today and the opportunities available to multiple generations. When we vote, we should look for leaders who understand their office and can see the community beyond it.

item.title: In Memory of Freddye Virginia VanHook
item.description:
On October 7, 2026, our mother, Freddye Virginia VanHook of Alamogordo, New Mexico, entered into her Savior’s presence.

Born in Independence, Missouri in 1935 to Fred Alexis Fitzgerald and Virgie Viola Fann Fitzgerald, she was raised in a loving Christian home along with her younger sister, Carol Lee Fitzgerald Ferrell. She loved sports and was an avid basketball and softball player. She cheered for the Kansas City Royals and Kansas City Chiefs every season whether they were winning or not.

Freddye graduated from Chrisman High School in Independence, Missouri and later, William Jewell College in Liberty, Missouri with a Bachelor of Science in Business. She loved music and singing and was in several choirs and groups while in college, where she also played on the women’s basketball team and was a member of Epsilon Pi sorority, an organization dedicated to leading young people to Christ. She was a faithful member of Bethel Baptist Church in Alamogordo, New Mexico where she loved singing in the choir. Her prayer and passion was for all of her family to have a personal relationship with Jesus Christ.

Freddye was preceded in death by her parents. She is survived by her husband, Thomas A. VanHook; her sister, Carol Lee Fitzgerald Ferrell (Bernal) of Independence, Missouri; daughter, Lisa White (James) of Independence, Missouri; daughter, Leslye Rallo (Joseph) of Saint Peters, Missouri; son, Paul Alexander “Alex” Donnell (Tandi) of Pleasant Hill, Missouri; daughter, Lynda Donnell of Alamogordo, New Mexico; 18 grandchildren; 24 great grandchildren; nieces and nephews; great nieces and nephews.

A celebration of life reception is planned for Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 2:00 pm at Bethel Baptist Church, 1316 N Scenic Drive, Alamogordo, New Mexico. In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation in Freddye’s honor to the Bethel Baptist Church music ministry.

item.title: In Memory of Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer
item.description:
Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer, age 94, passed away peacefully at her home in Alamogordo, New Mexico on Thursday, October 8, 2026.

A celebration of life service will be held at 11:00 am on Friday, October 16, 2026, in "the little chapel" at Christ Community Church in Alamogordo.

Adelin was born in Carrizozo, New Mexico on August 22, 1932. She cherished her early years growing up on her family's ranch outside of town before moving to Truth or Consequences, New Mexico where she graduated from high school. She went on to attend Texas Tech University, earning a Bachelor of Business Administration degree.

Following college, Adelin moved to Roswell, New Mexico where she met and married William Carl "Bill" Schauer. Together they raised two children, Leda and Tony. The family eventually settled in High Rolls Mountain Park, New Mexico surrounded by tall pine trees, apple orchards, trout ponds, and winter snows.

Following Bill's passing and as her children established their careers, Adelin pursued further education, earning a counseling degree from CBN University. She then dedicated many years to serving the emotional and spiritual needs of her community. In later years, she moved down the mountain to Alamogordo where she happily spent the last two decades of her active life volunteering for political events, enjoying lunches with friends, and deepening her fellowship within the local Christian community.

Throughout her life, Adelin was a devoted servant leader, serving as the Southern New Mexico Area President of Women’s Aglow Fellowship, President of Alamogordo Republican Women, and sharing her musical talents as an organist and pianist while teaching Sunday school at various churches.

Adelin is survived by her son, Tony Schauer and his wife, Linda; her grandchildren, Jessica, Thomas, Sarah, Cheryl, and Robin; nine great grandchildren.

She was preceded in death by her husband, Bill Schauer; her daughter, Leda Schauer; her beloved brother, Dewey Stokes.

item.title: Purple in the Park: Survivor Shares Path from Abuse, Addiction and Incarceration to Redemption 530pm Thursday
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Domestic violence survivors, families and community members are invited to gather Thursday, Oct. 15, at Washington Park for “Purple in the Park,” a free evening of awareness, education, fellowship, music and local vendors hosted by COPE (Center of Protective Environment) in recognition of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

The event runs from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. Attendees are encouraged to wear purple to show support for survivors. Light refreshments and entertainment will be provided. COPE’s message for the evening is “Listen. Believe. Support.”

Keynote speaker Grace Nagamine, a lifelong Alamogordo resident and domestic violence survivor, will share her personal story of abuse, homelessness, addiction and incarceration—and the path she has walked in the 18 years since that chapter of her life. Nagamine has publicly described surviving childhood abuse, domestic violence, substance abuse and time in the criminal justice system, experiences she has also detailed in her book The Grace Nagamine Story: Your Neighbor: Living the Fight. She has spoken of navigating systems including Child Protective Services as a grandparent, the welfare system as a mother in poverty, and the mental health system while dealing with personal trauma.

Those experiences now shape her advocacy. Nagamine founded Royal Angels, a nonprofit serving children with special needs that was inspired by her granddaughter Melanie. She has worked as a certified nursing assistant, served in the nursery at Mountain View Church for more than a decade, and is a former Mrs. New Mexico titleholder. She has publicly supported expanded funding for COPE and victim servicesWith Kids Inc and other advocacy organizations. 

COPE, which operates a shelter and provides crisis intervention, counseling, legal advocacy, safety planning and education across Otero and Lincoln counties, organized the park event as part of its annual Domestic Violence Awareness Month efforts. The agency’s mission is to help people affected by domestic violence and other forms of abuse through direct services and community education. Its 24/7 crisis line is 575-437-2673 (toll-free 1-866-350-2673).

Organizers describe the evening as an opportunity for education, resource information, fellowship and community connection, with local vendors and musicians contributing to the atmosphere. Washington Park has long served as a central gathering place for community events in Alamogordo.

The event is open to the public. Attendees are asked to wear purple as a visible sign of solidarity with survivors.

item.title: Dunn Solar Telescope Doomed from the Start
item.description:
Sunspot, Otero County N.M.- It appears that a faulty weld doomed the Dunn Solar Telescope at Sunspot before it started operating in 1969.

This is implied in the Dunn Solar Telescope Assessment conducted by SET Environmental of Milwaukee, WI, for the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), the parent organization for the National Solar Observatory (NSO). Alamogordo Town News obtained a copy of SET’s Feb. 5 summary report to AURA.

Demolition crews are reportedly on site now, and some science instruments may be lost because of contamination. This includes a new instrument developed by Queens University Belfast.

“Only a small number of items were recovered, decontaminated, and returned to their PIs [Principal Investigators],” NSF told ATN. “The DST continues to be an unsafe environment, and as this situation remains active, no further items will be recovered from the DST or the attached labs due to ongoing safety and environmental concerns.”

In its Feb. 5 report, SET wrote that a mercury drainpipe from the Dunn’s main bearing had a slow leak caused by a “faulty weld at the base of the cylinder” (emphasis added). When enough mercury leaked through the surrounding sleeve, it forced the weld open. This defect may have been there since the Dunn was built in the 1960s since weld repairs are not mentioned.

Sunspot Solar Observatory’s history starts in 1947 when two U.S. Air Force observers started observations to determine if it was a good spot for space weather forecasting. It quickly grew into a world-class solar observatory with its crowning achievement being the Vacuum Tower Telescope, later named in honor of designer Richard B. Dunn, which started operations in 1969.

(Sunspot was transferred to the National Science Foundation [NSF] in 1976 following a change in defense funding, and AURA was contracted to operate it. The land, however, belongs to the U.S. Forest Service, which has a say in the final disposition of Sunspot.)

The Dunn’s unique design — which inspired the designs of several later telescopes — included a main barrel hanging inside a concrete tower that is visible across the Tularosa Basin. This design kept the telescope straight and, with the observing platform attached to the barrel to stabilize images, let it rotate to follow the Sun across the sky.

To ensure smooth rotation, Dunn borrowed a technique from 19th Century lighthouses: mercury bearings. This was a key to the Dunn’s success and demise.

The Dunn had three bearings, from top to bottom: 1) a float bearing for the heliostat turret that followed the Sun, 2) a larger float bearing that supported the 250-ton main barrel and observing platform, and 3) a much smaller bearing almost 200 feet underground to stabilize the barrel just below the main mirror.

On Jan. 5, the large float bearing leaked about 186 pounds (roughly 6 quarts) of liquid mercury. New Mexico State University, then the operator, and NSO immediately closed the Dunn. Following that, Veolia Group, “a global leader in environmental services,” apparently was first to enter the Dunn and locate the leak. AURA next contracted SET to survey and determine the best entries and exits for a team to drain the mercury.

The eight-man team wore “level C Personal Protection Equipment [including] full face air purifying respirators equipped with mercury vapor cartridges, and hard hats.” They used a portable detector that shines ultraviolet light to measure mercury concentration in micrograms per cubic meter (a 3-1/4 foot cube) of air. One microgram is the weight of a grain of salt. Safety guides set the maximum safe level at 25 to 100 micrograms per cubic meter. Because mercury is six times denser than salt, a 100 microgram dot is narrower than a human hair.

While many people have briefly handled liquid
mercury (not a wise thing to do) without ill effect, the vapor is highly dangerous. Persistent handling lets the skin absorb it. Inhaling takes it straight to the bloodstream and the nervous system.

The team was inside the Dunn for just 25 minutes and found extensive mercury contamination. They recorded mercury vapor levels ranging from zero at a sewer manhole connection to 2,410 at a tunnel floor, 24 times the recommended threshold. More worrisome were readings up to seven times higher than the threshold in work areas: 260 in the lobby, 230 in the office hallway, and 700 in the kitchen/breakroom. The letter did not report readings for the observing platform.

Filtering the air is not a viable solution because surfaces can adsorb mercury: the vapor adheres and can easily be released. A 1982 study by the University of Auckland (New Zealand) showed that painted surfaces and vinyl flooring are strongest in this respect.

This led NSF to decide, on Feb. 26, that the safest option was draining and demolition. NSF contracted Thornton Tomasetti Inc. of New York with three sole-source contracts worth more than $13.7 million. The latest started Sept. 23 and runs through March 23, 2027.

At the Enchanted Skies Star Party outside Magdalena last Wednesday, astronomer John Briggs reported that a demolition contractor is on site. Briggs, who worked at Sunspot more than 20 years ago, was on site to remove key optical components from the Evans Solar Facility, which has two telescopes.

Briggs confirmed that the demolition plan is to dump most of the remains of the Dunn — which has three-foot-thick concrete walls — into the telescope pit, which is solid rock, and cap it.

Note: The author, Dave Dooling, is a veteran aerospace writer who was Sunspot’s education officer during 2002–12

item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Meeting Details — Oct. 13, 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission voted 6-0 Tuesday to put the city's last roughly $1 million in economic development funds toward clearing derelict buildings along White Sands Boulevard, after City Manager Bob Stockwell said most past grants from the fund failed to deliver lasting jobs.

The money comes from the city's Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) fund. Stockwell told commissioners the city has spent about $14 million on 22 LEDA projects since the tax was first imposed in 2001. Only three of those projects still operate in Alamogordo, he said; the rest defaulted, or met their commitments and then closed or left town.

"We don't look like a place, when you drive down those thoroughfares, where someone would want to invest substantially," Stockwell said, calling appearance the "common theme" in local economic development discussions.

His recommendation, which the commission adopted, directs him to work with the Chamber of Commerce and the Sacramento Mountains Foundation on a plan to use the public dollars to leverage private money for demolition and cleanup. Stockwell said the first project would likely be finishing demolition of the former Holiday Inn site, once the city receives title. He offered a second option, funding the remaining application from the Pineal Hotel and Bistro, but the commission did not take it up.

One commissioner abstained and left the meeting before the item was heard.

Commissioner Al Hernandez backed cleaning up the Holiday Inn site but questioned giving money to owners of other White Sands Boulevard properties, which he said sell for $25 a square foot and up. He suggested loans or a city purchase-and-resale arrangement instead. "It's taxpayer money one way or the other," he said.

Stockwell agreed the city should recover its costs where possible, calling the fund "seed money." He said the city should also consider bidding on tax-sale properties to get them into hands that will develop them. He noted that derelict properties are taxed at their run-down value, "so everybody's losing."

Mayor Pro Tem Josh Rardin asked for a consistent plan, saying the city has tended to "pick and choose" whom it goes after. He said the worst stretch of the boulevard runs between First and Tenth streets. Rardin also warned the money will not go far. "I bet the Holiday Inn is going to take half of it," he said, on top of $250,000 the city has already spent there.

Rardin opened a can of worms and committed an act of defamation against two property owners on New York Avenue asking whether earlier LEDA recipients on New York Avenue could be made to return money, Stockwell said recovery is unlikely when businesses fail. Both led a defamatory conversation that could lead to litigation.

Stockwell said the White Sands Theater received a $1 million check and "we don't know where that money is," adding that December is the first point at which the city can demand an accounting. He cited a $1.9 million default by Sunbaked Biscuits as another example.

More to come on this story later today in a followup story as the two property owners in question have been making payments, are well within the LEDA rules and have comment. Story to follow later today. 

There is no deadline to spend the remaining fund, Stockwell said. Hernandez made the motion; Rardin seconded it.

Stockwell, who said he has been on the job about 90 days, used his report to respond to social media criticism that he has not yet sent major water, sewer and street projects out to bid. He said no project will go to bid until its design is complete.

"As long as I'm the one sitting here, we are not going to bring projects to you or put them out to bid until, in fact, they are really ready to go," he said. "If that means I'm not very good at my job, then I'll take that."

He pointed to recent projects he said were rushed:

Stockwell said the next, already-budgeted phase of Oregon Avenue will be walked "inch by inch" before construction. Well-designed projects attract better contractors, he said, while poorly designed ones draw bidders who "think they're going to make good money on change orders."

Responding to a commissioner's question, Stockwell said the auditorium project is now out to bid. A pre-bid conference Tuesday drew 35 attendees, and the contract includes outside project management.

Hernandez, who said social media has also targeted commissioners with contracting backgrounds, thanked Stockwell. He said he watched "change order after change order" on the New York Avenue project and raised concerns about the cost of the city swimming pool, which he estimated at $16 million or more on a 25-year bond.

Bonito Lake. Stockwell said he met with the Lincoln County manager and the two agreed to study the hydrology of the post-fire watershed jointly, with the Forest Service. Ruidoso is predicting seven or more years of debris flows, he said. Recent rains overtopped the city's debris basins, sending silty water, but no debris, into the lake. The lake will stay open for fishing, but adding campsites is "premature," he said.

Lodgers' tax. The city is working with the Chamber of Commerce on whether to reinstate the lodgers' tax, which it previously canceled, and possibly contract tourism marketing to the chamber. Recommendations are expected in the next few months.

Toy Train Depot. The Sheldon Trust wants to fund a major reconstruction of the depot's tracks and buildings in exchange for a long-term lease. Stockwell said he expects to recommend the lease, with money set aside to restore the park if the volunteer-run depot ever closes.

Trash collection. The city's residential franchise with Southwest Disposal expires early next year. Staff are pricing alternatives, including a city-run system, and will report back within months.

Code enforcement. Stockwell said ordinance amendments are near a final draft. They would require owners to register vacant buildings, prove they are maintained and pay a fee. Other proposals include limits on vehicles per residential lot, keeping inoperable vehicles behind fences and keeping RVs behind the front of the house. "Half of the people will come in and praise what you're going to do, and the other half will want to lynch you," he said.

The RV issue came up earlier when a commissioner asked about an RV parked on a Sedona Ridge street for a month and moved slightly every 72 hours. Police Chief David Cunijaro said the current ordinance is vague and allows that practice. He offered to look into the address and the ordinance.

Hernandez renewed his call to require facades on at least three sides of new metal commercial buildings on White Sands Boulevard, Tenth Street, First Street and Indian Wells Road. Another commissioner asked that cleanup efforts apply citywide, not only between First and Tenth streets, and how the city would handle longtime owners and residents who will not sell.

The meeting opened with the swearing-in of the first members of the Mayor's Youth Advisory Commission, known as MAYAC. The Community Development Director introduced 16 students, and Municipal Judge David Overstreet administered their pledge to provide "a strong youth voice" and serve as a resource to the city.

Mayor Sharon McDonald said work on the commission began in March or April. She thanked volunteer mentors, the high school Interact club, the Rotary RYLA program and Alamogordo's high school and middle school. She also recognized a city staff member who helped launch the program and is now being treated for stage three cancer.

In public comment, resident K.D. Owens invited people of all political parties to this weekend's "No Kings, Vote Early" protest. She also asked the city to install a HAWK pedestrian signal on First Street near Avenida Amigo, or move the bus stop there.

Owens said that in the past two weeks a pickup nearly hit a wheelchair user who cannot get around the median, which has no cut-through, and a driver nearly hit a blind man in the crosswalk. In both cases, she said, a police officer stopped traffic. She said she will return "every week" until something changes.

Commissioner Stephen Burnett thanked crews for tree removal and other work at the golf course outside his district and the priority for him over district issues which he said is "looking very bright." New golf carts should arrive by the end of November.

The commission unanimously approved the agenda, with a planned executive session on litigation removed, and the consent agenda, both 7-0. Commissioner Robinson gave the invocation.

item.title: Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission Meeting Overview – Oct. 13, 2026
item.description:
TULAROSA — The Village of Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission spent much of its Oct. 13 meeting questioning a community solar developer about a draft land deal. It also found that the village has no agenda, minutes or applications on file for solar projects it appears to have approved for another company.

The commission took no action on either solar matter. Commissioners stressed that their role is to gather facts for the Village Council, not to approve projects. "We don't approve anything here," said one commissioner, addressed as Bucky, who led most of the questioning. "All our job is to do is to find facts."

The commission did vote to nominate two residents to fill vacancies, recommend approval of a short-term rental, and sign off on a roof permit that had already been completed.

Commissioners laid out the history of Sunvest's community solar proposals. Sunvest first came before the commission on Jan. 17, 2024. The minutes from that meeting say no action was taken and that a special meeting would be held two weeks later to decide.

Commissioners said a search turned up no agenda or minutes for that follow-up meeting. When Sunvest contacted the village recently, the company said it had already been approved. It sent four undated letters, signed by the mayor, covering sites it calls Tularosa One through Four.

Two of the letters say the village does not exercise zoning authority in the extraterritorial zone, so the sites fall under Otero County. The other two say the village approves the projects as utility structures under Section 154.25. A commissioner said one parcel number in those letters, R05564, could not be found in Otero County records.

"There's no file on any of this that we can find," a commissioner said. "There was no application submitted." The village also does not know whether Sunvest paid any fees. The commission has asked Sunvest to submit special use and zoning applications for the sites, and said the matter will go to the Village Council.

One commissioner questioned the mayor's letters. They said anyone building within the three-mile extraterritorial zone has to file with Tularosa as well as Otero County.

Cutter Brewer, senior developer for the southern U.S. at Reactivate, flew in from Houston to answer questions. Reactivate wants an option to lease about 35 acres of village-owned land for a community solar project. Brewer said the company is a startup of about two and a half years and a subsidiary of Invenergy. It has built and operates one project near Chicago.

Brewer said the project would fall under the New Mexico Community Solar Program, which caps projects at 4.95 megawatts. That usually takes 22 to 30 acres. The final footprint would depend on a PNM capacity study that could take months. He said the program's Nov. 1 deadline had been pushed to Feb. 1, though he had not yet received that in writing. If approved, he said, the company hopes to have the project running in about three and a half years.

Commissioners pointed to errors in the draft documents. The option agreement described 78.7 acres in Doña Ana County and cited Colorado law. Brewer called these template mistakes and said a corrected New Mexico version would be sent before any village vote.

The commission asked that several clauses be removed or changed:

Commissioners also asked for a decommissioning bond, village consent before the lease is assigned, and an ALTA survey and title commitment. They raised concerns that the developer could end the lease at any time while the village could not. Brewer said many of these points would be settled by lawyers when the lease is negotiated.

Commissioners also asked whether Tularosa residents would get priority to subscribe, and what they would save. Brewer said that is outside his role and agreed to bring someone who could answer.

The draft has been sent to the village attorney. Commissioners said it needs a redline review before it goes to the Village Council.

The commission reviewed a letter proposing an exchange: an easement over a ditch at 110 Central Avenue in return for the Stogden well lot near the Y. Commissioners said the letter was "literally all we have."

The questions they raised include:

The commission did not vote. It will prepare a findings of fact for the Village Council that lists the unanswered questions.

Two residents with long careers in construction introduced themselves as candidates for the commission. Efren Gonzalez cited about 25 years in construction and the low-voltage industry. David Gonzalez, a lifelong resident who is now retired, said he wants to help "beautify this place as it was before." The two are not related.

The commission voted unanimously to nominate both at the Village Council's Oct. 21 meeting. There will be two openings: Kim Skaggs has resigned, and Vice Chair Helton plans to leave in January.

Commissioners asked staff to find out where several items stand with the Village Council. These include the vacant building registration ordinance, a draft ordinance on development impact fees, and the Title 15 code enforcement schedule. They asked that these be placed on the council's old business.

On the Marino property abatement, commissioners said the owner remains incarcerated and is contesting a competency finding. The village attorney has advised waiting until a guardian ad litem is appointed. Commissioners called the property a fire hazard and said offensive material on it is visible to children. Staff will ask the attorney whether a partial abatement is possible now. Animals have been removed from the property.

The meeting ended with a presentation of roughly 40 minutes by resident Joan Price, a multimedia artist. She spoke on the Tularosa Village Historic District, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Price showed photos of restored adobes, the acequia, church traditions and newer walls and lighting she said are out of character with the district. She suggested a historic advisory committee and better promotion of the village's history.

Commissioners said they share her goals and want to adopt a historic preservation plan with ordinances. They asked her to reread the draft plan and send her recommendations in writing. The commission then adjourned.

The Village Council meets Oct. 21. It is expected to consider the two commission nominations and the Airbnb recommendation, and to begin discussing the Reactivate proposal.

item.title: Follow the Money: Block Cries 'Big PAC' While His Own PAC Pays His Own Company
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — In the race for House District 51, the two candidates are running very different campaigns.

Independent Grace Nagamine is talking about issues: power bills, veterans, seniors, CYFD reform.

Incumbent Rep. John Block is talking about Grace Nagamine's past — and about a mysterious "deep-pocketed, far-left PAC" he says is backing her.

There's just one problem with Block's story. He won't name the PAC. And the campaign finance records tell a very different story about who in this race is actually backed by big money.

In a fundraising email signed "John Block, NM House District 51, Republican, Otero County," Block writes: "I have an opponent this November backed by a deep-pocketed, far-left PAC that wants to elect Democrats up and down the ticket. Right now, that PAC has over $300,000..." The email asks supporters for $35 to $250 to help him hit a $9,500 goal.

No PAC is named. Nagamine's campaign filings back her up: as of her latest report, she has taken no PAC money — no direct contributions, no in-kind support. The only PAC dollars anywhere near her are the Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter's political action committee paying for its own endorsement of her on Aug. 29. An endorsement is not a donation, and it is not $300,000.

Full disclosure: one outside group has spent money for Nagamine — a grassroots volunteer organization based in Tularosa, which has put roughly $2,000 into independent expenditures supporting her in October after the most recent disclosure period

In a statement, a representative pushed back on Block's email directly: the group has raised about $218,000 this year across all of its various campaigns since November of 2025, but "the only money we have going against him is what the CFIS report" details — roughly $2,000 in the District 51 race of inkind contributions for targeted marketing. And on the position Block's email ascribes to the mystery PAC: "We do not believe in abortion up to birth! That is insane! He is such a liar!"

LTwo thousand dollars from local volunteers, and a direct denial from the only group spending a dime for her. That is the entirety of the "powerful PAC" operation behind Grace Nagamine.

Now follow the money on Block's side.

Piñon PAC is, for all practical purposes, Block's PAC. Its registration with the Secretary of State lists its address as 1111 Tenth St. #402, Alamogordo — the same address as Block's own Piñon Post LLC — and its treasurer is John Block. Its WinRed page solicits donations under his name: "Please join me in becoming a founding member… — John Block."

This year, according to Transparency USA's compilation of state filings, Piñon PAC paid Piñon Post LLC $4,673.80 — two payments of $2,336.90, on April 15 and June 4 — with no purpose disclosed

Money went from the PAC Block controls to the company Block owns. The PAC also took $2,000 from Block himself — check #1047, dated Jan. 10, 2025 — on top of $1,000 from his "John for New Mexico" campaign committee in Sept. 2024 and $5,500 from the committee in March 2024. It also reimbursed Block $148.55 for stamps and paid him $800 by check in April 2025. At the end of June, the PAC sat on about $31,600. The Secretary of State has been sent a note questioning the legitimacy of the payments to his blog which does no local advertising only ads via Google ads. 

John Block controlled, Piñon PAC has another benefactor: Our Values PAC, which sent $2,000 in February 2025 — the PAC's own filing lists Piñon PAC's payee address as 1111 Tenth St. #402, Alamogordo: Block's address. Our Values PAC is not a small local committee — its Secretary of State filings show it sitting on more than $355,000, after raising over $282,000 in late 2025. Its treasurer is listed as Anissa Tinnin of Albuquerque, a former executive director of the Republican Party of New Mexico, and the committee was originally registered in 2020 as the "Make New Mexico Great" political action committee. Her mother is Blocks state paid administrative aid. This is the sophisticated big-PAC money in the District 51 race — and it flows to Block's operation, not Nagamine's.

Piñon PAC's donor list reads like a House Republican caucus roster. Itemized records show contributions from fellow GOP legislators — Terrazas, Vincent, Mason, Zamora, Pettigrew, Reeb, Chatfield, Henry, Brown and Martinez — plus $4,500 from Rep. Stefani Lord in 2024

This is not a groundswell of Otero County constituents. It is Santa Fe politicians funding Santa Fe politicians.

And that money is being spent. Block's side has now put two costly mailers into District 51 mailboxes: his campaign's glossy postcard taking credit for millions in state spending — including money in bills he voted against — and Piñon PAC's hit piece on Nagamine's two-decade-old record.

District-wide mail is one of the most expensive things a legislative campaign can buy: design, printing, and postage to voters across the district, twice over. Piñon PAC's own filings show $1,370.10 paid to Greetings Etc Inc. for a "Mailer" in May 2026 — and in the 2024 cycle the PAC paid mail house North Rim International $7,355.69 for three mailers. (Public reports only run through June 2026, so the October hit piece's printing bill isn't in the data yet.) 

Blocks campaign is a big-money operation — funded by oil companies, corporations, allied PACs, and a $355,000 war chest — even as Block's fundraising emails ask grassroots supporters for $35 apiece to fight a phantom "deep-pocketed" PAC supposedly backing his opponent.

It is Piñon PAC that mailed District 51 voters the flyer dredging up Nagamine's 2005–2008 criminal record and calling her "too dangerous to be state representative" — an attack she had already defused two months earlier by disclosing the record herself in her August memoir, The Grace Nagamine Story given away to 100s of supporters and sold on Amazon. 

And what about Block's own campaign donors?

According to Money Trail NM's aggregation of state filings, the biggest checks to "John for New Mexico" this year came from oil and corporations: Permian Resources ($5,000), Devon Energy ($2,500), Presbyterian Health Plan ($1,000), Comcast ($500), Anheuser-Busch ($500) — plus PAC money from the Realtors and the optometrists. Individual local donors? Six of them, all under $100, the largest $93.69. In 2024, his top donor was Chevron at $11,700.

So the candidate Block, warning voters about a "deep-pocketed PAC" is himself funded by oil companies, corporations, and PACs — while asking grassroots supporters for $35 apiece.

The candidate he accuses has no PAC money behind her at all just inkind support that will appear in the next filing.

Meanwhile, Nagamine keeps talking about issues.

Her platform — published at graceforhd51.org with draft legislation attached — covers veterans and Holloman families, seniors and caregivers, CYFD reform, homelessness and mental health, small business, and roads and water.

Since August she has published step-by-step instructions for filing PNM billing complaints with the PRC and attorney general.

Block, who voted twice against the low-income utility rate bill (HB 91) and sponsored the failed 2026 tax on renewable generation (HB 113) which the state confirmed would have further raised PNM rates, skipped the issues and went personal instead.

Voters appear to have noticed. Learning of  the Piñon PAC mailer and before it landed, Nagamine posted an Oct. 13 video and commenters defended her as someone rebuilding her life; and one voter texted her campaign asking for 10–20 yard signs after receiving "that super crappy ad."

Block asked voters to follow the money. They did. It led back to him, and the big money politicians and corporate interests and sophisticated PACs that back him. We followed the money indeed as should the voters.
